pachomius.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
pachomius.name: Pachomius the Great
pachomius.feast_note: Western commemoration; Byzantine calendars generally use May 15, civil May 28 where Julian dates are followed.
biography: Pachomius helped establish organized communal monasticism in Egypt. After conversion to Christianity and a period of ascetic training, he founded a community at Tabennisi. His monasteries joined prayer, work, shared resources, and obedience under a common pattern of life.

The network grew to include multiple communities, and its rules influenced later monastic traditions. Stories of angelic instructions express the religious significance assigned to his work, but should not replace attention to the practical institutions he created. He died around the middle of the fourth century. Western calendars commemorate him on May 9, while Byzantine calendars generally observe May 15.

pacian-of-barcelona.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
pacian-of-barcelona.name: Pacian of Barcelona
pacian-of-barcelona.feast_note: Local and martyrological commemoration; May 9 was incorrect.
biography: Pacian was a fourth-century bishop of Barcelona whose surviving writings address baptism, repentance, and the identity of the Catholic Church. Jerome remembered him as a learned Christian writer. His teaching belongs to the effort to explain church life and reconciliation after baptism.

He corresponded with a supporter of the Novatian movement, defending the Church's authority to receive repentant sinners. These texts provide a more substantial basis for understanding him than later devotional anecdotes. His ministry shows how theological argument and pastoral care overlapped in the late Roman Church. He died around 390 and is commemorated on March 9, especially in the church associated with Barcelona.

pacificus-of-san-severino.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
pacificus-of-san-severino.name: Pacificus of San Severino
biography: Pacificus Divini entered the reformed Franciscans as a young man and became a priest, philosophy teacher, and preacher. His early ministry took him among communities in the Italian Marches. Over time, serious disabilities, including impaired mobility, hearing, and sight, restricted his public work.

He continued religious life within the friary, where accounts emphasize patience, prayer, and devotion to the Eucharist. He also served for a period as guardian despite his illnesses. Reported mystical experiences form part of the devotional record, while his long life with disability is central to his biography. He died in 1721 and was canonized in 1839.

padre-pio.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
padre-pio.name: Pio of Pietrelcina
biography: Pio of Pietrelcina was born Francesco Forgione and entered the Capuchin Franciscans. As a priest at San Giovanni Rotondo, he became known for celebrating Mass, hearing confessions, and offering spiritual counsel to large numbers of visitors. Reports of the stigmata and other extraordinary phenomena brought intense attention and ecclesiastical investigation.

His work also included support for the hospital known as the Home for the Relief of Suffering, linking prayer with practical care for patients. He died in 1968 and was canonized by John Paul II in 2002. His biography should distinguish documented ministry and charitable institutions from individual miraculous claims. The Church celebrates him on September 23.

paisios-of-mount-athos.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
paisios-of-mount-athos.name: Paisios of Mount Athos
paisios-of-mount-athos.feast_note: Orthodox feast; Julian July 12 corresponds to civil July 25 where observed.
biography: Paisios was born Arsenios Eznepidis in Cappadocia shortly before his family moved to Greece during the population exchange. He later became a monk on Mount Athos, where his life of prayer and counsel drew many visitors. His monastic career also included periods away from Athos.

People sought him for guidance about family life, suffering, and spiritual practice. Accounts of his discernment and reported miracles are preserved within Orthodox devotional tradition. He died in 1994 and was recognized as a saint by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2015. His teaching continues to circulate in collections of conversations and letters, and his feast is July 12.

pammachius.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
pammachius.name: Pammachius
biography: Pammachius was a Roman aristocrat and a correspondent of Jerome. He married Paulina, daughter of Paula, and after his wife's death directed his resources toward an ascetic and charitable life. Jerome's letters provide direct evidence of his place within a network of educated Roman Christians.

With Fabiola he established a hospice at Portus for travelers and people in need. He also participated in theological discussions, asking Jerome to address disputed teachings. His legacy therefore includes both practical hospitality and engagement with Christian learning. He died around 409 and is traditionally commemorated on August 30. His identity should not be reduced to later generic stories of noble charity.

pantaleon.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
pantaleon.name: Pantaleon
pantaleon.feast_note: Traditional Western and Byzantine feast; also known as Panteleimon.
biography: Pantaleon, called Panteleimon in Eastern tradition, is honored as a physician and martyr associated with Nicomedia. His later life story describes a doctor who embraced Christian faith and healed without demanding payment. He became especially important in devotion to saints associated with medicine and healing.

The martyrdom narrative contains elaborate miraculous episodes and should be treated as hagiography rather than a surviving contemporary court record. His cult was nevertheless widespread in both East and West, where he was included among the Fourteen Holy Helpers. His July 27 commemoration preserves the Christian ideal of compassionate healing joined to fidelity under persecution.

paschal-bayl-n.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
paschal-bayl-n.name: Paschal Baylón
biography: Paschal Baylón worked as a shepherd before entering the reformed Franciscans as a lay brother. His life in the friary emphasized ordinary service, poverty, and prayer. Although he had little formal education, people sought his counsel, and his devotion to the Eucharist became the most distinctive feature of his reputation.

Accounts describe courtesy toward visitors and generosity to people who were poor or afflicted. He died in 1592 and was canonized in 1690. Leo XIII later designated him a patron of Eucharistic congresses and associations, reflecting the lasting influence of his spirituality. His feast is celebrated on May 17, and Christian art commonly depicts him in Eucharistic adoration.

patrick.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
patrick.name: Patrick
biography: Patrick's own Confession describes his capture in Britain as a teenager and enslavement in Ireland. During those years he developed a deep life of prayer. After escaping and returning home, he eventually went back to Ireland as a bishop and missionary.

His writings also reveal the difficulties of his ministry, his defense of his vocation, and his concern for Christians subjected to violence and enslavement. They offer a stronger historical foundation than later stories about shamrocks or the expulsion of snakes. His precise chronology remains debated, but his role in Irish Christian history is fundamental. The Church celebrates him as Ireland's patron on March 17.

paul-chong-hasang.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
paul-chong-hasang.name: Paul Chông Hasang
paul-chong-hasang.feast_note: Roman memorial with Andrew Kim Taegon and the Korean martyrs.
biography: Paul Chông Hasang was a Korean lay Catholic whose family suffered in the early persecutions of the Church. As an adult he helped sustain the Christian community and traveled to China, where he sought clergy and formal ecclesiastical support for Korean believers.

His efforts illustrate the decisive role of laypeople in the origins of Korean Catholicism. When arrested in 1839, he submitted a written defense of the faith but refused to renounce Christianity and was executed. John Paul II canonized him in 1984 with Andrew Kim Taegon and other Korean martyrs. Their shared September 20 memorial honors a community spanning different social positions and vocations.
